retrieved_fault: Too Many Handovers (Signaling Overload);Extremely frequent handovers (perhaps due to a cluster of small cells or poorly tuned thresholds) are causing a lot of signaling and possibly overwhelming the RAN and even core with location updates. If UEs ping-pong or handover every few seconds (like vehicles passing many small 5G cells); the overhead can eat into capacity and CPU. This can be seen as a RAN resource exhaustion in terms of processing signaling and maintaining contexts for many HOs
retrieved_resolution: Review mobility logs: if you see same UEs handing over back and forth or moving through many cells quickly; identify if thresholds can be optimized: increase time-to-trigger for handover so brief good signal from neighbor doesn't immediately trigger; add hysteresis to avoid ping-pong; or if cells are too small for the speed (like a car crosses cell in seconds); maybe consider turning some cells to idle mode when not needed or rely on a macro layer for fast movers. Use features like conditional handover or dual connectivity if available: e.g.; in 5G; use multi-connectivity so that a fast-moving UE keeps connection to macro while using small cell; reducing hard handovers count. If signaling is the main concern; possibly restrict how many handovers per minute a single UE can do (some networks have implicit clamp; but not standard). Check if some handovers are unnecessary (like triggered by spurious measurements or false pilots maybe interference making neighbor look good when it's not). If so; adjust the measurement filtering. After tuning; monitor handover success and ping-pong rate success should remain high (we don't want to stop needed handovers) but ping-pong count should decrease. The RRC connection drop rate may improve because fewer handover failures in ping-pong scenarios. Also the control plane load on that cluster of cells should drop; freeing capacity for actual new connections or data. Possibly also battery life of UEs in that area improves (less signaling means less power usage on their side too)

retrieved_fault: UDM communication failing due to certificate issue
retrieved_resolution: There appears to be a security or trust issue between the UDM and other network components. If the UDM does not trust the credentials or certificates from other services (or those services do not trust the UDM) secure communication will fail. This often occurs due to an expired certificate or a certificate mismatch or misconfigured security settings. This results in TLS handshake failures or rejected connections. Verify the certificates and security configurations on the UDM and the peer entities (such as the AMF or AUSF). Ensure that the UDM certificates are valid and not expired and that they are recognized as trusted by the other components. Likewise confirm that the UDM trusts the certificates of its peers. If any certificate is expired or untrusted then install a valid certificate and adjust the trust settings accordingly. Once the security settings are corrected the UDM should be able to communicate securely with other network functions.

retrieved_fault: UDM unreachable from AMF

Functions like the AMF cannot retrieve subscriber information or perform authentication when the UDM is offline or unreachable. Check the health and status of the UDM service. Ensure that the UDM application is running and that there is network connectivity between the UDM and other core network functions (like the AMF and AUSF). If the UDM process has stopped or crashed then restart it and observe if it begins responding to queries. Also verify that the UDM is properly registered in the network service registry (NRF) so that other components can discover it.

If the AMF is not connecting due to a certificate mismatch or TLS handshake error it means the secure communication between the AMF and another core component is failing. This could be caused by an expired certificate a trust configuration error or inconsistent security settings between the AMF and its peers. To resolve this verify the certificates and security settings on the AMF and the corresponding network function it is communicating with. Ensure that the AMF certificate is valid and trusted by its peers and that it trusts the peer certificates as well. Update any expired or incorrect certificates and align the TLS configurations on both sides. Once the certificate issue is fixed the AMF should be able to establish secure connections normally.

retrieved_fault: What happens if NFVi experiences hardware failures?
retrieved_resolution: Hardware failures in NFVi can cause simultaneous outages of multiple CNFs; leading to service disruptions across network slices. For example; server crashes may impact AMF/SMF/UPF functions simultaneously; resulting in registration failures and data session drops.

retrieved_fault: What happens during NFVi storage failures?
retrieved_resolution: Storage failures impact stateful CNFs like UDR; causing subscriber data unavailability. This leads to authentication failures (AUSF/UDM errors); session context loss in SMF; and policy enforcement failures in PCF.

retrieved_fault: What happens during NFVi resource contention?
retrieved_resolution: Resource contention (CPU/memory/I/O) causes CNF performance degradation - increased AMF authentication latency; SMF session setup delays (>50ms impact); and UPF packet jitter. Severe cases trigger Kubernetes pod evictions; leading to service interruptions.

retrieved_fault: What is NFVi in 5G infrastructure?
retrieved_resolution: NFVi (Network Functions Virtualization Infrastructure) provides the hardware and software resources (servers; storage; networking; hypervisors; container orchestration) that host 5G CNFs. It enables cloud-native deployment through virtualization and containerization; supporting dynamic resource allocation for network slicing and service agility.

retrieved_fault: UPF not handling large packets properly
retrieved_resolution: The UPF is likely dropping packets due to an MTU or fragmentation issue. retrieved_fault: AMF session capacity exhausted leading to session setup failures

In this scenario the AMF is essentially out of resources for additional connections. To fix this check the AMF resource utilization and licensing status. If a limit has been reached you may need to increase the capacity by adding more resources or obtain a higher-capacity license. Additionally ensure that stale sessions or inactive users are cleared from the AMF so they do not consume capacity unnecessarily.

Consider scaling out by distributing sessions to another SMF instance or upgrading hardware if the SMF is at capacity. Optimizing the configuration or applying software updates could also help improve how the SMF handles heavy load.

Check the MTU settings on the UPF and along the path to the data network. Ensure that MTU values are consistent or that the UPF is configured to fragment packets when necessary. If there is an MTU mismatch adjust the MTU on the UPF or other network devices to a uniform value. Test with large packet sizes after aligning the MTU settings to confirm that the UPF no longer drops packets due to fragmentation issues.
